clue.text: —— Down his flashing eyes we read in 13 down

definitions.text: —— Down his flashing eyes we read in 13 down

parts.words: —— Down his flashing eyes we read in 13 down
parts.note: a gap-fill: Coleridge's poem warns twice of the poet with 'flashing eyes', and the missing warning word fills the blank

explanation.surface: A line about flashing eyes, quoted from the poem at 13 down.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge's Kubla Khan ends 'Beware! Beware! His flashing eyes, his floating hair!'; the clue quotes the line with the warning left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation's omitted word is a cautionary exclamation telling the reader to be on guard.

clue.text: Dog on a hill taking care …

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the noun: the person whose job is taking care of a collection

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A dog perched on a hilltop, minding something.
explanation.walkthrough: TOR is a craggy hill in the West of England, such as those on Dartmoor.
explanation.definitionFit: A museum's keeper is the person entrusted with the care of its collection.

clue.text: A lovely South Londoner, but flighty

definitions.text: A lovely South Londoner, but flighty

parts.words: A lovely South Londoner, but flighty
parts.note: the 'lovely Londoner' is not a person but a butterfly named after a district of south London, and 'flighty' means it flies

explanation.surface: A pretty girl from south London with a fickle streak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lovely' and 'flighty' suggest a fickle young woman; the subject is a butterfly first recorded in the south London district of Camberwell.
explanation.definitionFit: The butterfly takes its name from the London district where it was first found and is prized for its handsome wings.

clue.text: Sir Thomas Browne wrote of his garden

definitions.text: Sir Thomas Browne wrote of his garden

parts.words: Sir Thomas Browne wrote of his garden
parts.note: Browne's 1658 treatise is titled after the garden of a Persian king

explanation.surface: A remark about the seventeenth-century writer Sir Thomas Browne and a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Browne's work 'The Garden of Cyrus' (1658) studies the quincunx pattern in plantings.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian king named in the title of Browne's treatise is the garden's owner.

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for the man whose name the letters form

indicators.note: the island's name makes the man's name when its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The island of Minorca is responsible for a certain man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' tells you the seven letters of Minorca are rearranged into the radio pioneer's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points to an individual man, here the Italian inventor of wireless telegraphy.

parts.note: read not as a compromise but as a dish served between the main courses of a meal

explanation.surface: Taking a compromise path between extremes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A middle course' suggests moderation; it is a dish served between courses, French for 'between dishes'.
explanation.definitionFit: This French dish is a side or sweet served between the principal courses of a dinner.

clue.text: This Berkshire town seems to spurn youth

definitions.meaning: a market town in the Vale of the White Horse, historically in Berkshire
split into two words, the name reads as desiring old age, as if rejecting youth

explanation.surface: A Berkshire town appears to turn its back on young people.
explanation.walkthrough: The town's name split as WANT AGE says 'desire age', which is what spurning youth would mean.
explanation.definitionFit: The town is a real Berkshire place, and its name read as two words expresses a wish for old age.

clue.text: Tall fees for little bits of literature.

indicators.note: the fodder is exchanged for its rearrangement, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Paying high charges in exchange for snippets of reading matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is the only signal: the eight letters of 'Tall fees' are rearranged into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Handbills and pamphlets are small printed items handed out to readers.

parts.note: Hope is the novelist Anthony Hope, who invented a fictional kingdom; 'him' is an inhabitant of it

explanation.surface: A man whose spirits were lifted by hope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope' is not optimism but the novelist Anthony Hope, author of The Prisoner of Zenda, set in his invented kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Anthony Hope's imaginary Central European kingdom is a creation of that author.

parts.note: the opening line of Coleridge's poem with the place name left blank, and two other words referred to other lights

explanation.surface: The first line of a famous Romantic poem with words missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge's Kubla Khan opens 'In Xanadu did Kubla Khan / A stately pleasure-dome decree'; the blank after 'In' is this answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in the quoted line is the place where the Mongol emperor's pleasure-dome stood.

clue.text: They might be as slow as Lent

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase could become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Things that could be as sluggish as the season of Lent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' tells you to rearrange the ten letters of 'slow as Lent'; a batsman who stonewalls scores slowly, which gives the clue its double sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points to defensive barriers, or in cricket the slow blocking innings that a dull batsman plays.

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a male
a lot is an item put up at an auction

explanation.surface: A man sold off under the hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a Spartan serf was a man who could be bought and sold.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spartan serf was an unfree labourer, owned and so traded like goods.

parts.note: things that hold blades the way a sheath does, but which sit on a dining table

explanation.surface: Scabbards, apart from those found at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: A sheath holds a blade; at the dinner table the blade is held by small supports on which the cutlery is laid.
explanation.definitionFit: These small table supports keep a dining blade off the cloth, doing a scabbard's job of holding it.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'See 10' only points to 10-across, where these words fill a gap in a quoted line; the light has no definition or wordplay of its own to annotate

parts.note: universal means applying to all
solitude is the state of being without company

explanation.surface: Wondering whether everyone is lonely.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue serves as definition and wordplay: complete solitude is being entirely by yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: Being completely by oneself is total, universal isolation.

parts.note: crows are dark-feathered birds, yet they are not the species whose name is those two words joined

explanation.surface: A paradox about crows.
explanation.walkthrough: Crows are black birds, written as two words, but they are not the thrush-family songbird written as one.
explanation.definitionFit: The common European songbird, the male jet-black, has a name that describes crows too.

parts.note: 'men' are not people but large knives and forks for cutting meat, which rest on table supports

explanation.surface: Some men are lying on something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'men' points to people who slice a joint, but the word also names the large knives they use, which rest on knife rests at table.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both people slicing a roast and the big knife and fork used for slicing.

clue.text: He's called raw, perhaps, because he's had no firing

definitions.text: He's called raw, perhaps, because he's had no firing

parts.words: He's called raw, perhaps, because he's had no firing
parts.note: raw clay or pottery is unfired; a new soldier is called raw because he has not yet fired a weapon

explanation.surface: Something called raw because it has never been fired, like pottery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firing' suggests a kiln, where pottery is fired; the raw one is a new soldier who has not yet fired a shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A newly enlisted soldier, untrained, is described as raw.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'See 10' only points to 10-across, where this word fills a gap in a quoted line; the light has no definition or wordplay of its own to annotate

clue.text: These are often seen in flight

definitions.text: These are often seen in flight

parts.words: These are often seen in flight
parts.note: a flight is a set of stairs, not air travel

explanation.surface: Things commonly spotted while flying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' suggests birds or aircraft, but a flight is a staircase.
explanation.definitionFit: A staircase is made of individual stairs, which make up a flight.

clue.text: Not made by 11, says the poet

definitions.text: Not made by 11, says the poet

parts.words: Not made by 11, says the poet
parts.note: Richard Lovelace wrote that solid barriers of masonry do not make a gaol

explanation.surface: A poet's verdict on something that is not built by walls.
explanation.walkthrough: Lovelace's 'To Althea, from Prison' says 'Stone walls do not a prison make'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet's line names a gaol as the thing stone walls do not create.

parts.note: 'relative' means over relatives: heads of families rule their kin

explanation.surface: People who hold power only in a limited sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relative rule' suggests limited authority, but it is rule over one's relatives, as by the head of a family.
explanation.definitionFit: Male heads of families or tribes govern their kin.

parts.note: a plain description of something turning or skidding sideways

explanation.surface: Something veers off course.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn or slide sideways off course is to veer suddenly.

parts.note: a spring water containing lithium salts, once drunk as a remedy

explanation.surface: A bottle of mineral water.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is given to a spa water rich in lithium salts.

clue.text: Not the headquarters of the Commons Preservation Society

definitions.text: Not the headquarters of the Commons Preservation Society

parts.words: Not the headquarters of the Commons Preservation Society
parts.note: the society protected common land; the parliamentary Commons sit in a chamber with a different name

explanation.surface: A building that is not the base of a society saving common land.
explanation.walkthrough: The Commons Preservation Society protected common land; here 'Commons' is Parliament's elected chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Commons is the elected, less senior chamber of the British Parliament.

clue.text: Caroline, -" the ugliest girl in Hammersmith," wrote Boz

definitions.text: Caroline, -" the ugliest girl in Hammersmith," wrote Boz

parts.words: Caroline, -" the ugliest girl in Hammersmith," wrote Boz
parts.note: a gap-fill from Dickens's Sketches by Boz, which names a schoolgirl at a Hammersmith boarding school

explanation.surface: Dickens describing an unattractive girl from Hammersmith.
explanation.walkthrough: Boz is Dickens's early pen name; in 'Sentiment' from Sketches by Boz, Miss Caroline Wilson is 'the ugliest girl in Hammersmith'.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank is filled by the girl's surname in Dickens's sketch.

parts.note: not siding with someone but impersonating them, playing their role

explanation.surface: Someone backs another person in a dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes someone else's part' suggests supporting them; it means pretending to be them.
explanation.definitionFit: To impersonate is to assume another's identity or play their role.
